# Open Scientific Problems Worth Attacking With a Frontier Model — Final Ranked Report

## Bottom line

**The survivor set is empty. There is no ranking to give.**

Twelve candidates were scored (totals 24–28 on a 30-point scale) and all twelve were killed during skeptical refutation. This is not a formatting accident and it should not be read as "the pipeline found nothing, try harder next time with the same net." It is a signal about the *class* of problem the prospecting stage was selecting for. The most valuable output of this run is therefore the closing section, not the (absent) ranking.

A note on the graveyard record below: each killed entry carries the `killCondition` it was written with, but the refutation record does not preserve the adjudicating argument. So the one-line notes are the **fatal exposure** each candidate carried — the thing that made it killable — not a verbatim transcript of the kill. Treat them as sufficient grounds not to re-list the problem, and if a future run wants to resurrect one, the burden is to show that specific exposure is closed, with evidence, *before* scoring it.

## What the killed set has in common — read this part

Nothing survived, so the reusable finding is about the *shape of the net*, not the catch. Four structural facts, in descending order of importance for the next run.

### 1. Every candidate belonged to one of two archetypes, and both archetypes have a systematic failure mode

**Archetype A — the normalization play** (#1, #3, #4, #8, #11, #12; arguably #2).
Form: "The field is stuck because *n* papers report the deciding quantity in incompatible units/conventions/protocols. Rebuild them onto one axis and the dispute becomes arithmetic." The stated model edge is thankless cross-paper bookkeeping that no specialist will do because it isn't publishable on its own.

This is a genuinely good instinct and it is why these scored highest. But look at the kill conditions: **every single one is a precision or coverage condition that cannot be evaluated until you have already built the table.** "Kill if protocol variance dominates." "Kill if no model has both numbers." "Kill if δ¹³C uncertainty spans the discriminating gap." "Kill if the papers report J only as figure points." The archetype's characteristic pathology is that *the go/no-go test costs 70% of the project*. Worse, the base rate is bad: if normalizing the data were going to resolve the dispute, the reason twenty papers didn't converge is usually that the underlying measurements genuinely lack the resolving power — not that everyone forgot to convert units. Convention chaos is often a *symptom* of an underdetermined measurement, not the cause of the stalemate.

**Archetype B — the compute-frontier play** (#5, #6, #7, #9, #10).
Form: "This is stated as open but the obstruction is engineering. Reimplement the known-correct search with better symmetry breaking / a better encoding / a smarter solver and push one step past the frontier." Verifiability is perfect (5/5 on #6, #7, #9) because the certificate is machine-checkable.

Also a good instinct, and the verifiability is real. But the failure mode is arithmetic and it is nearly universal: **published frontiers sit exactly where someone competent already spent the available constant factors.** A model reliably buys 2–10×; the next step in these state spaces costs 10–1000×. #5 states this explicitly (n=16 is ~10× the n=15 state space); #7 states it explicitly (machinery is two orders short); #9 states it explicitly (reachable orders likely already cleared). The one entry that escaped the pure-compute framing (#6, by pivoting from the 381-block design to the 334-block code record) escaped it by *changing the target*, which is the right move — but it then landed on a different wall, the possibility that the symmetry-reduced instances are already solved to optimality.

### 2. The scoring rubric saturated and did no discriminating work

Totals ranged 24–28 across twelve candidates — a 4-point spread on a 30-point scale, with the top scorer killed like the rest. `resourceFree` was 5 for ten of twelve; `selfContained` was 4 or 5 for all twelve. Those two axes cost 10 of the 30 points and carried essentially zero variance, because the prospecting stage was *already* filtering on them before scoring. All real variance lived in `verifiability` (2–5) and `searchShape` (2–4).

Consequence for the next run: **stop spending rubric weight on axes the prospecting filter already enforces.** Score on the axes that actually vary, and add the axis that would have killed this entire batch cheaply — see below.

### 3. The missing axis: cost-to-kill

Not one of the twelve had a decisive test that could be run in the first hour. In several the `firstMove` and the `killCondition` are the same activity. That is the defect that produced a 0/12 run: twelve problems were carried to full scoring and full theory-of-attack write-up when a cheap probe would have eliminated most of them at the prospecting stage.

The next run should add and heavily weight:

> **Cost-to-kill:** Can the project's central assumption be falsified by a bounded action — one download, one lookup, one calibration run against a known answer — that costs a small fraction of the full attempt? Score 5 if yes and the probe is specified concretely. Score 1 if the kill test requires building the deliverable.

Note which candidates would have scored well here: #5 (calibrate against published V₇(15) — genuinely cheap and genuinely decisive), #6 (reconstruct the known 333-block record from its published group), #9 (check the ETP repo for the enumeration ceiling before writing any encoding). Those are the right *shape* of first move even though the problems died. Every Archetype-A candidate would score 1–2.

### 4. Verifiability below 4 should be an auto-reject, not a deduction

#12 scored `verifiability: 2` and its own theory of attack says why: "a botched normalization produces a confident-looking exclusion that is wrong." A problem where the failure mode is *a wrong answer that looks right* is strictly worse than no attempt, because it consumes the run and emits a false result into the record. Same structure at `verifiability: 3` for #4, #8, #10, #11. Treat 5 as the target, 4 as acceptable with an explicit external checker named, and ≤3 as disqualifying regardless of total.

## Positive specification for the next prospecting run

Look for problems with **all** of the following, and prefer them over anything scoring higher on the old rubric:

1. **The checker is external, cheap, and pre-existing.** A truth table, a rank computation, a Lean kernel, a held-out dataset the claim was not fit to. Not "a careful audit trail."
2. **The bottleneck is neither compute nor measurement precision.** If the honest one-line diagnosis of why the problem is open is "nobody had enough CPU" or "the instruments can't tell," skip it — a frontier model changes neither. The bottleneck you want is *nobody assembled these two literatures* or *nobody tried the obvious thing because it was beneath a specialist's time*, **combined with** confirmable-in-advance sufficiency of the inputs.
3. **Data sufficiency is verifiable before the work, not after.** The single strongest filter. If you cannot confirm in under an hour that the public inputs carry enough resolution to separate the hypotheses, the problem is Archetype A and it will die at hour 40 instead of hour 1.
4. **There is a genuine out-of-sample test.** #8 was the only candidate with one (fit 2019–21, predict 2022–25 against data postdating the disputed papers) and that feature is worth more than any other single property on this list. Prefer disputes where one camp made a dated, reversible, now-checkable prediction. Prospect specifically for *claims with expiry dates*.
5. **Partial results bank.** Prefer problems that decompose into independently publishable lemmas, so a stalled run still emits something. #12 had this property and was still correctly killed — it is necessary, not sufficient.
6. **A smaller adjacent target exists.** #6's pivot (attack the 334-block code record, not the Fano-plane analog) is the single best structural move in this batch and should be a standing prompt: *for any famous open problem, is there a tracked incremental record adjacent to it whose certificate is short?* Records on maintained tables are underrated targets — they are refereed, unambiguous, and moving one is a real result.

**Concretely, prospect in these directions next:** dated predictions from one side of a live dispute that have since become checkable; entries on maintained record tables (coding bounds, combinatorial design tables, circuit-complexity records, verified-value tables) where the record-holder's method is published and its exploited symmetry is narrow; claims in refereed papers that rest on a control the authors never ran *and where the control set can be assembled from public data whose sufficiency is obvious on inspection*; and cross-registry consistency checks where two independent public repositories should agree and no one has checked.

**Avoid:** "the units are inconsistent, so let me rebuild the table" (unless data sufficiency is confirmable up front); "the search stopped for memory reasons" (unless a ≥10× state-space reduction is identified *before* committing); and anything whose deliverable is an opinion about which of two papers is right.
